newsitem.title: USA: Marathon presses ahead with Ruhrgas suit.
newsitem.headline: Marathon presses ahead with Ruhrgas suit.

text.p: Marathon Oil Co is pressing ahead with allegations that Germany's largest natural gas company conspired to monopolize the Western European gas market, an attorney representing the Houston company said on Monday.

Marathon has asked a U.S. appeals court to revive its civil lawsuit alleging Germany's Ruhrgas AG conspired with Norway's state-owned oil and gas company Statoil to monopolize the Western European natural gas markets since the 1970s, Marathon attorney Clifton Hutchinson said.

The lawsuit was dismissed in March 1996 after a federal court in Houston ruled that the German company could not be sued there, but Marathon has asked the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans to overturn that decision.
"This case is not dead," said Hutchinson, an attorney with Dallas law firm Hughes & Luce LLP representing Marathon.

Marathon, a unit of USX-Marathon Group, has sought to recover $300 million it spent to develop the Heimdal gas fields in the North Sea, plus four times that amount in punitive damages from Ruhrgas, Germany's largest gas company.
Ruhrgas spokesman Klaus Walther over the weekend said the Essen-based company fulfilled the terms of its contract with Marathon and that the group would win in the appeals court.

Marathon in the suit alleged a Ruhrgas-led consortium in a series of closed-door meetings agreed with Statoil to monopolize control of Norwegian North Sea gas by linking the fields into a single pipeline terminating at a Ruhrgas facility in Emden, Germany.

The consortium then enticed license holders from three northern North Sea fields to connect to the pipeline system by offering premium prices for the gas that it never intended to pay, Marathon alleged in federal court papers.

"Both Statoil and Ruhrgas fraudulently concealed their secret agreements from Marathon," Marathon said in court papers. "Had (Marathon and its subsidiaries) known the truth about Ruhrgas' and Statoil's relationships and plans, they would never have agreed to commit hundreds of millions of dollars to develop the Heimdal field and to support a pipeline to Europe that landed in a facility controlled by Ruhrgas."
Marathon said Ruhrgas has since blocked its attempts to sell gas from the fields to other buyers by refusing to provide information on pipeline transportation costs.
